1:
The argument against idolatry is finished, a new section opens with a new speaker, and the first question is who he is. Gill rejects both readings he inherits, that the voice is Cyrus and that it is the prophet, and takes it for Christ summoning the islanders. Wesley agrees that the prophet speaks in Christ's name, and Henry, hearing the isles as the Gentiles, notes that they listened when the Jews were deaf. Ellicott holds the figure in tension: the Servant is at once identified with Israel, in fulfilling its ideal, and distinguished from it, as its Restorer and Redeemer.

Keil and Delitzsch account for that tension by making the term contract. At its widest circumference the servant of the Lord is all Israel; at a smaller circle the true people contained within the nation, the kernel inside the shell; here it goes back to its very centre, and the servant is the heart of Israel, from which salvation flows first through the veins of the people of God and then through the veins of the nations. Clarke argues hard for the Messiah and then declines to close the case: whatever Vitringa and Lowth have proved, he doubts whether the prophet, Cyrus, and the Messiah may not each be intended in turn, the earlier shadowing out the later, and holds that the literal sense should be sought first.

On the mouth made a sharp sword the voices agree that the weapon is speech. Wesley takes it of the word made quick and powerful, the polished arrow piercing deeper for its brightness. Ellicott finds in it the spiritual nature of the Servant's victories, and reads the hiding in the quiver as reserve, the shaft kept back until the hour was come. Henry takes the hiding as both concealment, the calling of the Gentiles long veiled under the ceremonial law, and protection. Clarke alone leaves the Bible to defend the metaphor, quoting the comic poet on the sting Pericles left in his hearers and Pindar's habit of calling his own verses shafts, and judges the figure bold but just.

The address of the Servant as Israel is treated as a title rather than an identification. Ellicott observes that Israel began as an individual name and should be so once more in one truly a prince with God, and would render the next clause in whom I will glorify myself. Wesley compares the way a royal name descends to successors and calls Christ the great Israel of whom the patriarch was a type. Clarke says flatly that a name won by contending with God cannot belong to the prophet.

The confession of fruitless labour startles Ellicott, who admits the accents of disappointment sound strange from the lips of the true Servant, then makes them part of the discipline of every servant in proportion to the thoroughness of his service, illustrated in the prophet of Anathoth and fulfilled at Gethsemane. Henry turns it to the use of ministers who have spent themselves for nothing: the cause is righteous whatever the success, and the reward is with God though the fruit is not. Wesley reads the judgment claimed as the Servant's right, secured by promise and purchase.

The clause about Israel not being gathered divides the tile textually. Clarke reports that manuscripts and the marginal correction read to him rather than not, and that several versions drop the negative altogether; Ellicott calls it a transcriptional error and would read that Israel be gathered to him; Keil and Delitzsch render it positively. Wesley and Henry keep the negative and take the verse as consolation under failure. Clarke adds that the word for the preserved of Israel is much doubted, one version reading it as the branch. All agree on the enlargement that follows, that raising the tribes was the lesser errand and the light to the nations the greater.
7:
A fresh oracle opens with the speaker named by his titles, which Gill takes for the Father's, addressed not to the prophet or the nation, as his predecessors held, but to Christ. The one addressed is at the bottom of humiliation. Ellicott renders the phrase literally as despised of soul, allowing either that soul stands for men or that the contempt enters into the soul of the sufferer; the point is that the doer of the great work is despised by the world and by his own people, and yet he and no other will accomplish it. Wesley finds it fitting Christ exactly in the days of his flesh, abhorred by his own nation and so far from a temporal monarch that he paid tribute. Henry presses the servant of rulers to its lowest sense, one crucified as a slave, and reads the rising of kings as fulfilled when the great of the earth submitted to his yoke.

Clarke works the same verses as a textual critic. He suspects a lost letter before his Holy One, the preceding word ending in the same consonant; he thinks the participle for despised should stand in the passive form the sense requires; and at the summons to those in darkness he counts the manuscripts that supply a conjunction.

On the acceptable time Ellicott gives the literal season of good pleasure and makes the Servant the link of a new covenant, an idea developed later by the prophet of Anathoth. Keil and Delitzsch have him heard when he prayed out of the bondage to the world he shared with his people. Wesley concedes the limits of that hearing: not to deliver him from death, but to crown him with glory. Henry makes the covenant clause the heart of it, the Servant given not merely as mediator but as all in all, the whole duty of the covenant summed up in our being his and the whole privilege in his being ours.

How far the release of the prisoners is spiritual divides them. Gill takes the prison threefold, of sin, of the law, and of Satan, the covenant blood being the discharge; Wesley reads the prisoners as Gentiles bound by the cords of their sins. Ellicott holds the deliverance of Israel the more prominent here, though the words have a wider application, and Keil and Delitzsch likewise confine the verses to Israel. Ellicott keeps that restraint over the desolate heritages, allowing a literal fulfilment partly accomplished under Zerubbabel while we look to the spiritual inheritance.

The march home is drawn out by Henry, whose flock feeds on highway ground and bare high places, sheltered from the heat and led by the water out of the rock rather than rain pools. Ellicott notices that the word for heat is the one used elsewhere of parched ground and stands for the mirage of the scorching desert. On the levelled mountains Gill thinks of the ranges between Babylon and Judea; Ellicott hears in the pronoun a claim of universal lordship.

The land of Sinim scatters them completely. Ellicott takes it for the furthest edge of the prophet's horizon, excludes the Sinites of Canaan and the Egyptian Pelusium, and reports modern scholars almost unanimous for the Chinese, adducing commerce and porcelain found in Egyptian ruins. Wesley offers the Sinites or Sin in Egypt standing for the south; Henry guesses a province of Babylon not elsewhere named. Clarke derives the name from a root meaning bush, concludes the land is woodland, and asks whether the lost tribes are not among the peoples of Africa and America whom Europeans think they have a right to enslave. All join in the closing summons: Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch have the whole creation called to the chorus, Gill hears the angels in heaven and the saints on earth, Henry the creature's earnest expectation.
14:
Against all that has been promised Zion answers that she is forsaken, and the voices treat the complaint gently. Wesley calls it an objection: how can these things be true when the church is in so desperate a condition? Gill would rather render it as a pluperfect, for Zion had said, and though the words fit the captivity he takes Zion for the church under the gospel. Keil and Delitzsch have the prophet looking back on the suffering from the standpoint of deliverance while it still runs on, so that what follows speaks to the church of the exile. Ellicott makes the sharpest connection: Zion shared the misgivings felt even by the Servant himself, but did not rise out of them into assurance as quickly as he did.

The reply is the mother and her child, and each voice presses a different part of it. Gill notes the accumulation: an infant rather than a grown child whose disobedience might cool affection, and the phrase son of her womb added because a woman may nurse a child not her own. Keil and Delitzsch make the love far greater than a mother's, and Ellicott observes that maternal love survives in the most depraved, yet even this may perish while the divine pity cannot. Henry takes the question in two steps: it is not likely a mother should forget, the child being helpless and a piece of herself, yet it is possible, for she may be dying or unnatural; so the compassion promised exceeds the tenderest nature knows.

The engraving on the palms divides them along a line of custom. Clarke takes it for a real practice, marks punctured into the hand or arm and made indelible by fire or staining, some sign of the city or temple, as pilgrims to the sepulchre are still marked. Ellicott makes it the almost universal practice of tattooing, by which a man carried the name of his god, the outline of his home, or the face of one he loved, and draws the anthropomorphic consequence that God could not open his hands without being reminded of her. Henry and Wesley reject any such reading for the homelier custom of a string tied on the finger or a keepsake ring worn for an absent friend; some, Henry adds, apply the engraving to the wounds of the crucified.

Whether Zion's children are rather her builders stays unsettled. Clarke reports that the ancient versions read bonayich, thy builders, and that the Talmud directs the same, and presses it further than anyone: the parallel clause should then mean the destroyers become her offspring, the usual rendering being flat after their zeal has just been described. Ellicott accepts the builders but keeps the destroyers going out. Keil and Delitzsch grant that the antithesis favours builders, then decide for sons, since that suits the verses following and the thought of children rebuilding the walls follows from the antithesis anyway. Gill reads the sons as young converts flocking in.

The rest is amazement. Ellicott has the widowed daughter of Zion unable to believe the crowding children are hers, and compares the mother who pointed to her sons as jewels better than a rival's gems. Clarke thinks the bride clause has lost a word, since a bride binds on ornaments and not children, and finds it supplied in the Greek. Henry marks the surprise: she never bore pain for these nor took pains with them, yet has them reared to her hand. Who the lost children were is disputed. Wesley and Henry take them for the Jews cut off by unbelief and the later ones for the Gentiles who came in their room; Gill denies this outright and makes the lost those destroyed by persecution and the later ones the converts gathered when antichrist falls; Ellicott keeps to the words and calls them the children of Zion's bereavement.
22:
The answer to Zion's astonishment is that the nations will fetch her children home. Keil and Delitzsch note that the prophecy steps backward in the future to explain the manner of the return, and that the raised hand and the planted signal are both favourite figures here: the nations read the mark and obey, carrying the sons as a foster-father carries an infant. Ellicott observes that both words in the verse are used of the heathen, summoned by that signal to their work as nursing fathers. Wesley hears a general gathering his forces, and takes the sons for those who become Zion's by adoption. Henry reads the lifted hand two ways, as a beckoning to those the day-long stretched-out hand had not reached, or as almighty power exerted to make them willing, the standard being the gospel preached; and he turns the carrying into a rule, that those concerned with young converts deal with them as tenderly as the promise does.

Kings as nursing fathers is where the tile divides. Gill refuses the figurative reading, which took the royal titles for apostles, and insists on kings and queens literally, part-fulfilled in a Persian king and a Jewish queen, more fully in Christian sovereigns, and reserved for the latter-day glory. Henry names the same monarchs and adds that whenever the sceptre is put into religious hands the promise is fulfilled, the church here being in an infant state. Ellicott keeps the force of the image: kings ordinarily gave their children to nobles to rear, and Zion is to have the sovereigns themselves. Keil and Delitzsch make it a test of governments, since all that is true in the regal headship of the church will be realised here and all that is false in regal territorialism will condemn itself.

Clarke will have none of it as prediction. He gathers the eastern usages behind the licking of the dust: the Persian court that admitted no one without the act of adoration, the Macedonians prostrating themselves before a king intoxicated with success, and a conquered prince who kissed the prints of his enemy's horse and made verses saying the mark in the dust served him now for a crown. Such images, he concludes, are general amplifications drawn from the manners of the country, not predictions to be fulfilled according to the letter. Wesley notes the same practice without pressing the point.

The doubting question that follows is read by Gill either as the boast of the nations or as the prophet objecting in the people's name, and by Ellicott as Zion speaking in her little faith. Its second phrase splits the tile textually. Clarke calls the received reading a palpable mistake and would put the terrible one where the righteous stands, the correspondence between question and answer requiring it and two versions supporting it. Ellicott finds neither available sense quite satisfactory and inclines to the same emendation, which fits the parallelism of the next verse. Keil and Delitzsch resist it: the parallelism does not compel the change, the oppressor cannot be called righteous since he is wicked, and the phrase means no more than a host of captives belonging to the righteous. They identify the giant as the Chaldean, not the Persian. Wesley and Henry find no difficulty, taking the captivity lawful because the justice of God pleads against release, and the ransom what answers it.

The close is agreed. Ellicott notes the emphatic pronoun, the question answered because God himself delivers, and reads the oppressors eating their own flesh as the self-destroying collapse of Zion's enemies. Henry has the ruin begun by invasion and finished by division, blood given for blood. Gill denies any famine is meant and expects the mutual slaughter to be verified among the Popish party; Clarke sees the persecuting powers at last ceasing to destroy the church and destroying one another instead.
